contracts.description: loom's MCP transport as behavior: a request/result envelope identical across HTTP and stdio (transport-neutral), total dispatch (every registered tool resolves or returns a typed error envelope, never an uncaught throw), an oversized-payload guard, and a security boundary expressed as refusals — reject unauthenticated calls when a token is set, refuse to bind a non-mesh/public interface, and never dial outbound to serve a call. The literal bind address and the Tailscale topology are deployment (recorded in the portable-MCP ADR), excluded here. Forethought / to-be for loom (github.com/jbarket/loom).

exclusions: The literal bind address, port, and Tailscale interface selection: where loom listens is deployment (the ADR), not behavioral contract. The contract is that it REFUSES a public bind, not which mesh address it picks.

The HTTP wire framing itself (chunking, keep-alive, TLS termination) and the MCP protocol version handshake mechanics: binding surface. Only the envelope's logical shape and the transport-neutrality of results are contract.
MCP-App / ui:// resource serving is a FUTURE extension of this contract (the felag-board pattern applied to loom), deliberately out of this 0.1.0 — it lands once the base transport conforms.
goals: TO-BE (forethought): loom's network surface as observable BEHAVIOR — the MCP request/result envelope, total tool dispatch, typed error envelopes, a guard against oversized payloads, and crucially transport-NEUTRALITY (the same call over HTTP and over stdio yields the same result). This is the 'how you reach loom' layer that unlocks the chat surface (spear -> one over the mesh).

TO-BE: the security boundary, also as behavior — loom rejects unauthenticated calls when a bearer token is configured, refuses to bind a public/0.0.0.0 interface (only loopback or the mesh interface), and never initiates an outbound connection to fulfill a call. The Tailscale address itself is deployment (the ADR), not contract; the REFUSALS are contract.
Authored before the impl: loom is stdio-only today. These criteria are proposed and carry no evidence — the fixtures are the target L3 builds to, then each is ratified active as it goes green.
name: loom-transport

body: loom answers MCP calls with a result envelope whose LOGICAL shape is identical whether the call arrived over stdio or over HTTP — the transport is a carrier, not a semantic. A tool call that returns content C over stdio returns the same content C over HTTP for the same inputs and store state (transport parity). Malformed input yields a typed error ENVELOPE (a structured { error, reason } result), never an uncaught throw that crosses the transport boundary, and never a 500 with a stack. This is the to-be generalization of loom's current single-transport surface.
title: The envelope is transport-neutral

gherkin:
Given a well-formed tool call over HTTP and the identical call over stdio against the same store state
When each is served
Then both return a success envelope with the same logical content — the transport does not change the result (transport parity)

Given a tool call with malformed arguments
When it is served over either transport
Then loom returns a typed error envelope ({ error, reason }) — never an uncaught throw or a raw stack crossing the transport boundary

body: Every registered tool name resolves to a handler or returns a typed 'unknown tool' error envelope — dispatch is a total function over the tool namespace, with no panic path. An unrecognized tool, a tool with a missing required arg, and a well-formed call are three distinct typed outcomes (refused-unknown, refused-bad-input, ok), each a value not a throw. Oversized request payloads (beyond a configured cap) are rejected with a typed envelope before the handler runs, so a hostile or accidental megabyte can't wedge the daemon.
title: Dispatch is total; payloads are bounded

gherkin:
Given an unknown tool name, a known tool missing a required argument, and a well-formed call
When each is dispatched
Then the unknown name returns a typed 'unknown tool' envelope, the missing-arg returns a typed bad-input envelope, and the well-formed call is served — three typed outcomes, no panic path

Given a request payload larger than the configured cap
When it arrives
Then loom rejects it with a typed oversized envelope BEFORE the handler runs — a too-large request cannot wedge the daemon

body: loom's reachability boundary is expressed as behavior loom can be tested for. When a bearer token is configured, a call without it (or with a wrong one) is REFUSED with a typed unauthorized envelope, and a call with the correct token is served — the auth gate. loom refuses to bind a public or 0.0.0.0 interface: a configuration asking it to listen on a non-loopback, non-mesh interface is rejected at startup (bind-safety) — the 'never expose my brain to the internet' itch made a startup invariant. And loom never initiates an OUTBOUND network connection to fulfill a tool call (no cloud callback) — every answer is computed from local stores. Where it actually binds on the mesh is deployment; that it refuses the unsafe binds is contract.
title: The boundary is refusals — auth, bind-safety, no callback

gherkin:
Given a bearer token is configured, and calls arriving with no token, a wrong token, and the correct token
When each is served
Then the no-token and wrong-token calls are refused with a typed unauthorized envelope and the correct-token call is served — the auth gate

Given a startup configuration requesting a bind on a public/0.0.0.0 interface, and one requesting loopback or the mesh interface
When loom starts
Then the public/0.0.0.0 bind is REFUSED at startup (a hard invariant) and the loopback/mesh bind is accepted — loom cannot be made to expose itself to the internet by config alone

item: loom never initiates an outbound network connection to fulfill a tool call: every tool answer is computed from local stores (memory.db, knowledge.db, identity markdown) with no fetch/callback to an external service. A conforming implementation has no code path where serving a call opens a socket to a remote host — the boundary is inbound-only.
